archetype.name: Rebuilding (pressure defense, unfinished offense)
archetype.definition: A third straight bottom-tier Titans team with a front that gets home and a passing game that has only just started to show signs of life, playing for development more than for the standings.

report.headline: Worse record than play, but still a bottom-five team waiting on Ward
report.take:
This is the third straight lost season in Tennessee, after 3-14 finishes in 2024 and 2025, and the profile has not changed much. A net EPA of -0.135 ranks 28th, the offense is 27th and the defense 25th, and the Titans keep the ball less than anyone in the league at 25.63 minutes a game. Cam Ward has started every week, with Tony Pollard as the clear lead back and Carnell Tate and Wan'Dale Robinson splitting the top targets. The roster has a few real pieces. It does not yet have enough of them.

The defense is a split personality. Up front it is legitimately good: a 26.2% pressure rate ranks 4th, and it tackles as well as almost anyone, with a missed-tackle rate 2nd in the league. Behind that rush the coverage leaks, especially underneath. EPA allowed on short passes ranks 30th, the explosive pass rate allowed ranks 29th, and opposing WR1s have scored 6.4 PPR points a game above their usual output, 31st. Offenses also run against Tennessee more than the situation would predict. That reads less like a soft run defense, since rush EPA allowed is a middling 15th, and more like game script: opponents get ahead and lean on the ground. The quarterback gets hit, but the receivers get open.

The 1-7 record overstates how bad the team is. The point differential implies 2.5 wins, wins over expected sits at -1.54, and the Titans have won one of six one-score games while covering half their spreads. Saleh has also gone for it on every fourth down that qualifies, which makes for a high-variance team. The offensive line is stranger than its sack numbers suggest: a 4.6% sack rate ranks 7th, but a 25% pressure rate ranks 30th. Ward is escaping a lot of trouble, yet drives still stall, and 12 turnovers in eight games keep wiping out the good stretches.

The most encouraging trend is recent. After passing EPA of -16.9 against Houston in Week 5, Ward posted +5.9 against Cleveland's 11th-ranked defense and +8.7 in a 36-43 shootout at Cincinnati. That is two games, not a breakout, but it is the first sustained positive passing in this sample. The schedule ahead offers several soft defenses (Dallas 31st, Detroit 30th, Las Vegas 28th), so a couple more wins are realistic. The ceiling is still low while the pass defense gives up this much underneath.

strengths.title: A pass rush that gets home
strengths.body: Tennessee pressures quarterbacks at the 4th-best rate in the league and has 20 sacks. The rush produced six sacks against Indianapolis and three at Cincinnati, so this is not one fluky game. Pressure is the most stable part of this roster, and it travels against any opponent.

strengths.title: Sure tackling limits the run game
strengths.body: A 5.3% missed-tackle rate ranks 2nd, which keeps rush EPA allowed in the middle of the pack even though opponents run on this team a lot. Good tacklers do not usually go cold. This is part of why the defense rarely gets gashed for long touchdowns on the ground.

strengths.title: Passing game finally trending up
strengths.body: Ward's last two games produced the two best passing-EPA days of the season, including 304 yards at Cincinnati. One came against a top-12 defense, so it is not purely schedule. The early-season floor was very low, which is why this is a trend to watch rather than a settled trait.

concerns.title: Underneath coverage is getting picked apart
concerns.body: Short passes against Tennessee are among the most efficient in the league, and opposing top receivers feast. This is the cost of a defense built around getting after the quarterback: quick throws beat the rush before it arrives. The 43 points and 462 passing yards allowed at Cincinnati show how ugly it gets against a good passing offense. Nothing on the injury report suggests a fix is coming, and Marcus Harris's ankle could make it worse.

concerns.title: An offense that can't hold the ball
concerns.body: The Titans rank 31st in yards per game and last in time of possession. A heavily pressured line and a below-average rushing EPA keep putting the defense back on the field. Time of possession has been the worst in the league all year, so this has been structural, not a few bad games. The recent passing uptick is the only real counter-evidence.

concerns.title: Turnovers erase the good drives
concerns.body: Twelve giveaways in eight games, with at least two in six of them, have undercut the offense even on its better days, including the Cleveland loss. The defense's takeaways keep the margin close to even. The giveaway rate is still too high for a team with this thin an offensive margin to win close games.

trend.note: The offense has climbed from 3 points against Houston to 24 against Cleveland and 36 at Cincinnati, and the Titans covered as big underdogs in two of their last three. The defense has gone the other way in the same stretch, which tempers the read.

nextGame.headline: Rested Titans need deep shots against a Jaguars defense built underneath
nextGame.body:
Jacksonville arrives at 6-2 with the league's best point differential, the 2nd-best net EPA, a top-five offense and a defense 3rd against both pass and run. The Book has Tennessee as a 10.5-point home underdog in a division game. The matchup has one clear crack: the Jaguars are the stingiest team in the league on short passes but 27th on deep ones, and tight ends and lead backs get nothing against them. Tennessee's best path is Ward pushing the ball downfield to his wide receivers. The danger runs the other direction too: Jacksonville's efficient passing game meets a Titans defense that ranks 30th on short throws.

Tennessee comes off a bye with 14 days of rest, but the report is heavy. Carnell Tate, the team's leading target, is out with a shoulder injury, and Tyjae Spears and punter Tommy Townsend are also out. Starting guard Peter Skoronski and right tackle JC Latham are both questionable, and corner Marcus Harris is questionable with an ankle. Linebacker Dorian Mausi is back from injured reserve. Jacksonville is essentially healthy, with only a safety inactive as a coach's decision, and Trevor Lawrence has started every game.

waysToWin.title: Attack Jacksonville's soft deep coverage
waysToWin.body: Jacksonville smothers everything short but gives up big efficiency on deep throws. With Tate out, Robinson and Elic Ayomanor have to win vertically, and Jacksonville has also been leaky against WR3s. Ward's last two games suggest he can hit those throws.

waysToWin.title: Rush and steal possessions
waysToWin.body: The Titans' 4th-ranked pressure rate faces a Jaguars line that allows pressure at a middling rate. Pressure is how Tennessee forced four takeaways at Cincinnati. Short fields are the realistic way an offense this limited gets to 24-plus.

waysToWin.title: Fourth-down aggression shortens the game
waysToWin.body: Saleh has gone for it on every qualifying fourth down. Against a heavy favorite, extending drives and draining clock limits Jacksonville's possessions. It is a high-variance plan, which is exactly what a 10.5-point underdog needs.

waysToLose.title: Lawrence carves up the underneath zones
waysToLose.body: Jacksonville passes efficiently, and Tennessee is near the bottom of the league against short throws. Quick passes neutralize the Titans' rush before it lands. If Harris is limited at corner, Jacksonville's top receiver could have a big day.

waysToLose.title: Giveaways feed the takeaway leader
waysToLose.body: Jacksonville leads the league in turnover margin per game and ranks 3rd in takeaways. Tennessee has given the ball away 12 times. Two turnovers against this team likely end the game early.

waysToLose.title: Short-handed line, no easy outlets
waysToLose.body: If Skoronski and Latham can't go, a line that already allows pressure at the 30th-ranked rate faces a top-seven pass rush. Jacksonville also takes away tight ends and lead backs, so Ward's checkdowns to Gunnar Helm and Pollard dry up. Drives stall, and red-zone trips become field goals against the 4th-ranked red-zone defense.

nextGame.watch: Whether Ward keeps taking the deep shots that Jacksonville's coverage allows, now that Tate is out and the short game is closed off.

restOfSeason.body:
The underlying play points to a few more wins than the record shows. A point differential worth 2.5 wins and a one-score record this poor tend to drift back toward the middle. The schedule also includes several bad defenses: Dallas, Detroit and Las Vegas are all bottom-five on that side, and Indianapolis and Washington are winnable at home. The recent passing surge is the swing piece. If Ward's last two games are the new baseline, the offense moves from bottom-five toward the low 20s in points.

What probably won't change is the pass defense. The rush is real, but short-area coverage has been bad all year, and good passing teams (two Jacksonville games, Detroit, Houston) will keep scoring. Expect a team that loses fewer games by double digits and steals two to four more wins. That is still a bottom-five finish, which fits a rebuild.
swingFactors: Whether Ward's recent passing efficiency holds
Health of Skoronski, Latham and Tate

confidence.note: Eight-game sample, a two-game offensive uptick that could be noise, and key injuries on the line and at receiver.
